# 12-transload: sources

Back-test entry `12-transload.yaml`. Transload, YC Spring 2026 (Launch YC 2026-05-18; Launch HN 2026-06-09). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **HN**: Launch HN thread, founder post and replies. https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48463273 (read whole through the HN Algolia API, https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/48463273)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QP2-transload-we-measure-freight-with-security-cameras
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/transload
- **TTN**: Transport Topics, "Precision Pricing" (carriers' dimensioners in terminals). https://www.ttnews.com/articles/precision-pricing
- **FW**: FreightWaves, "Gov't lawsuit against YRC shines light on LTL reweighing practices". https://www.freightwaves.com/news/ltl-suit-against-yrc-spotlights-reweighing-practices
- **DTS**: Diversified Transportation Services, "How does a dimensioner work in a real-life environment". https://www.dtsone.com/dimensioner-actually-work-real-life-environment-2
- **SMC**: SMC³ blog, "Where LTL dock operations can improve shipper/carrier relations". https://smc3blog.com/where-ltl-dock-operations-can-improve-shipper-carrier-relations/

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the practitioner role, `dock_supervisor`; context actor).**
- HN: "transload helps LTL trucking companies measure freight dimensions using the security cameras already installed in their terminals." and "In practice, many terminals only measure a sample of their shipments."
- TTN (Estes): "A dockworker uses a forklift to drive the freight up to the landing zone".
- *My choice:* no public source names a job title (the shortlist scores this item 2 for that reason). I chose the **dock supervisor**, the person who runs a shift on the cross-dock and decides which freight goes to the dimensioner. That is where "only measure a sample" happens. A dock worker scans but does not decide what gets measured, and the revenue team only sees the result later.

**2. What (the job).**
- HN: "If a shipment is larger than the shipper reported, the carrier undercharges for it while still giving up the same amount of trailer space."
- HN: "carriers lose money every day because shippers understate dimensions and LTL is priced by volume."
- Job wording ("get every shipment billed at its true size without slowing the dock") is mine, combining these quotes with item 3's congestion point.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- HN: "The obvious fix is to measure every shipment, but thats impossible in a busy freight terminal. Dedicated dimensioning systems work for freight that passes through them, but they add forklift travel, create dock congestion, and change the normal flow of work."
- TTN: "We dimension a little more than 35% of our freight" (Estes). YRC about 40%, Oak Harbor about 8%.
- *My choice:* occasion "dock shift"; recall window 5 working days; Frequency 4 to 5 working days out of 5. The source says it happens on every busy shift but gives no count.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- HN reply: "Our wedge is underbilling in LTL trucking with ~10k relevant cross-docking warehouses across the US and Europe."
- YC-L: over 2 million irregular items move across the US by truck every day (as read on the page).
- *My choice:* market US. The company is based in Munich, but the US is the market its posts name first. Segment: dock supervisors at LTL carriers' cross-dock terminals in the US.

**5. Who pays (decision-maker role, buyer and payer, purchase friction).**
- HN: "We are currently working with several LTL carriers." YC-C: "transload helps logistics companies measure shipments using the security cameras they already have." YC-L asks: "Do you know any trucking company or warehouse owners?"
- *My choice:* the carrier pays. The **terminal manager** chooses (role id `manager`), and head office has to agree. Public material does not say who signs.
- Purchase friction, tested "An IT review of camera access": my choice. HN (kotaKat) gives a nearby signal: "you may need to look into NTEP approval before this is being used for legal trade... dimensioning is a big deal." Shared camera footage is the step most likely to need sign-off.

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- HN: "Our system has two main steps: connect a barcode scan to the right object in the video, then estimate that object's dimensions in real-world units."
- HN: "Dock workers already scan freight as part of the normal workflow. Each scan gives us a timestamp and a handling-unit ID."
- HN: "identify under-dimensioned shipments, attach visual evidence, and help carriers correct the billing or classification."
- HN: "Nearly every warehouse already has CCTV." Compatibility tests whether the cameras cover the doors where freight is scanned. That condition is my choice, because the mechanism needs it.
- Adoption friction, "Review each shipment the system flags": my choice. The output is a flag with evidence, and someone on the dock or in billing has to act on it.

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- HN reply: "We're seeing ~$50k/site/month in recoverable revenue from fixing that alone."
- YC-C: the founders put catching these differences at about $50k per site per month in rebillings and improved trailer utilization (as read on the page).
- *My choice, derived from the value claim:* no price is public. The founder's price belief is **$4,000 to $6,000 a month per terminal**, about a tenth of the $50k claim, the share a value-priced B2B tool commonly takes. The cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$30,000 to $50,000 a month**. The top is the founders' $50k. The low end allows for the HN post's "roughly 10%" mis-measured against YC-C's "15%" (10/15 of $50k, rounded down). Ability to pay is derived by code: 8% to 20%, small share.
- `hourly_rate` $30: my choice, a round figure for an LTL dock supervisor's loaded hour. No source gives one.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- HN: "After spending time with customers and talking to more than 50 trucking companies, we realized that forklift routing was not the pain people kept bringing up. Freight dimensions were."
- HN: "For one customer, roughly 10% of checked shipments had dimension errors."
- HN: "Jago grew up close to this industry through his family's LTL trucking and cross-docking business."
- YC-C: "For our customers, 15% of shipments turn out to be bigger than what the sender claimed."

## The respondents

No public first-person account by an LTL dock supervisor or terminal manager was found. HN has no commenter who works on a dock, and searches of trucking forums and Reddit returned nothing on dimensioning. The shortlist warns not to invent customer voices. So **every story below is the author's invention, filling that gap**. Each is built on the trade-press facts named after it, and no real person's name is used.

Dock supervisors (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Marcus Bell: author's invention, filling a gap: no dock account public. Built on HN ("many terminals only measure a sample") and TTN (dimensioner lanes, Estes' 35%).
- Rosa Delgado: author's invention, filling a gap. Built on HN ("add forklift travel") and TTN (a disputed pallet a dimensioner photo showed was "72 inches tall").
- Dwayne Okafor: author's invention, filling a gap: the sceptic whose terminal already dimensions a large share. Built on TTN (Estes "a little more than 35%", YRC about 40%, "there are no long waiting lines").
- Teresa Lindqvist: author's invention, filling a gap: a small terminal with no dimensioner. Built on HN (sample only) and DTS ("Carriers base the size on the longest measurements in each direction").
- Hamid Rahimi: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Kenji Watanabe: author's invention, filling a gap. Built on FW: the dock staff "in charge of reweighing the freight" were separate from the "weigh and research department". So he picks the escape "Someone else does the checking".
- Lakisha Freeman: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). The sensitivity is grounded in FW's account of a federal lawsuit over reweighing practices.
- Brian Kowalczyk: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (no shift with unmeasured freight in the window).
- Priya Nair: author's invention, filling a gap: a terminal with a dimensioner on every inbound door, one down for an hour. Built on TTN (Estes "multiple units at our facilities").
- Samuel Mensah: author's invention, filling a gap: peak volume blocks the lane. Built on HN ("create dock congestion") and TTN (YRC: "we don't want a dockworker sitting and waiting on a dimension machine").
- Graciela Ortiz: author's invention, filling a gap: nothing measured, found at the trailer. Built on HN ("still giving up the same amount of trailer space") and SMC ("you're seeing more and more reclassifications on carriers' docks").
- Jerome Whitfield: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

Terminal managers (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only, no story by rule):
- Alan Brooks: author's invention, filling a gap: a manager whose own audit roughly matches HN's "~$50k/site/month".
- Fatima Benali: author's invention, filling a gap: counts the cost as inspection staff hours, not lost revenue (FW: a weigh and research department of "between 80 to 90 people" at one carrier).
- Ray Castellano: author's invention, filling a gap: cannot put a number on it, and head office decides.
- Nadine Fournier: author's invention, filling a gap: a smaller terminal with a smaller loss.
- Oluwaseun Adebayo: author's invention, filling a gap: a large hub where the loss is above the founders' figure.
- Greg Halvorsen: author's invention, filling a gap: the manager whose dimensioners already catch it and who sees no cost (TTN: Estes "using 129 dimensioners", "payback timeline is three to six months").
- Mei Lin Chou: author's invention, filling a gap: a mid-size loss and a long IT review.
- Dale Pruitt: author's invention, filling a gap: counts re-measuring hours, and someone else had to agree.

## Open

- **No job titles in the public material.** The dock supervisor and the terminal manager are my choices (item 1, item 5). A back-test may find the founders would have named the carrier's revenue or pricing team as the payer instead.
- **Price is derived, not stated.** $4,000 to $6,000 a month and the $30,000 to $50,000 cost are my derivations from the $50k value claim. Treat the commercial vector's reading as a reading of my derivation as much as of the founders' belief.
- **All twenty respondents are invented.** No dock or terminal manager voice was found in public. The stories are grounded in trade press (TTN, FW, DTS, SMC) and in the founders' HN post.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The founders' benefit is labelled "Every undercharged shipment caught, not just a sample" under the nearest code, `easier_recovery` (revenue recovery). The label carries the meaning; the code name is approximate.
- **Decision-maker role id is `manager`.** The checker builds the Buyer and payer sentence from the role id ("The manager decides, and head office has to agree."), so the id was shortened from `terminal_manager`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional for a back-test. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM HOLDING_UP, SOLUTION PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Compatibility: camera access needs help or is missing at 3 of 7), COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice: most managers see far less than $30,000 to $50,000 a month).

screens.why_b3: The card names and belief lines are the ones I checked, in my words: true size, paperwork size, measuring a sample.

screens.why_b2: The question says what is counted, the strip shows seven cells over a 0 to 7 axis, and the marker sits at 6, so all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: "Prevalence" and the 8 in 10 line are recognisably my problem in dock terms, but this belief isn't among the two listed as checked on the way in, and the wording is Keel's.
screens.why_b4: The So line sends me to the next two cards for frequency and importance, which is a useful pointer, but it doesn't say what this result means for the idea or what I should do.
screens.why_b5: The claim stays with "these 7", the n is visible and the small group is called "a lean, not a call", so nothing stretches to all dock supervisors.
screens.instead: So line: All 7 found oversized freight in the last 5 working days, so the problem exists on these docks, but that doesn't show it costs enough to fix; check the next two cards for how often and whether it matters before leaning on this, and talk to more supervisors because 7 is only a lean.

screens.why_b3: Frequency and 4 to 5 working days out of 5 are the belief I set, and "a shipment bigger than its paperwork said" is how my dock supervisors would say it.
screens.why_b4: "Whether it matters is the next card" points me onward correctly but does not say what a near-daily oversize finding means for my idea or what I should do with this lean.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible and "a lean, not a call" is honest, but the bold "Holding up" with a bar met exactly by 4 people, one more against flipping it, is a soft overstatement next to that caveat.
screens.instead: Holding up, but only just: 4 of the 5 people I could count find an oversized shipment on 4 or 5 days of 5, right at the bar, so one more answer could flip it; treat it as a lean and get more supervisors before relying on it.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "4 of 5 put it in their two · bar 4 of 5 · at the bar", so I have both the answer and the number that decides it.

screens.why_b3: The Importance name, my belief line and "billing freight at its true size" are exactly what I checked on the way in.

screens.why1: As a first question it makes sense: it checks straight off whether I've dealt with undersized paperwork on my dock this week, which is the whole reason you'd talk to me.
screens.why2: I get it on first read, but we'd say a shipment was 'under-declared' or 'cubed out over the BOL', and 'bigger' doesn't say whether it means dims, weight or both.
screens.why3: I run the shift and hear about it from the dimensioner or my dock guys, and most freight never gets measured, so I can answer for what got caught but not for what went through unchecked, and 'you' could mean me personally or my dock.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but 'I can't recall one particular shipment' is odd for a yes-or-no about a whole week since we see this all the time, and 'I'd rather not say' is a second escape when one should be enough.
screens.why5: It reads like a question about my dock's freight, with nothing about anyone's product or plan coming through to me.
screens.why6: The question is short and the 'Yes or no' is easy to catch, but the spoken form drops both escape chips, so what I hear doesn't match what's on the screen and I'm not told I can say I can't recall.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did your dock catch a shipment measuring bigger than its bill of lading said? Yes; No; or say I can't recall.

screens.why1: I just said yes to finding one, so asking how many days that happened this week is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: Plain on first read, though on my dock I'd say the freight cubed out bigger than the BOL rather than 'paperwork'.
screens.why3: I run the shift and see the dimensioner exceptions and reweighs, so I can count the days I worked, though only for the freight we actually measured.
screens.why4: Having already said yes, 1 to 5 covers every true answer without overlap, and 'I can't recall' fits a supervisor who doesn't keep count day by day.
screens.why5: It's a plain question about my week and nothing about a product or company reaches me.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and 'a number from 1 to 5, or say you can't recall' is easy to hold after hearing it once.

screens.why1: After two questions on oversize freight, it makes sense to ask where that problem ranks against everything else I dealt with on the dock.
screens.why2: Wrong door, short-staffed, claims, trailers out on time and true size are all how we talk on the dock, and I get it on the first read.
screens.why3: I run these shifts and deal with all five of these every week, so I can pick one from last week without guessing.
screens.why4: These are real, distinct headaches and None of these fits, but billing is the one that sits a little off because a dock supervisor gets freight measured while the billing itself happens in the office.
screens.why5: It keeps the job of billing freight at its true size, sits it among ordinary dock problems, and shows me no product or company language.
screens.why6: It is one short question with five short options read as a list and one escape at the end, so I can hold it and answer after one hearing.
screens.instead: Think of your last week on the dock. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Finding freight sitting at the wrong door; getting freight measured at its true size; running the shift short-staffed; handling damaged freight and claims; or getting trailers loaded and out on time. Or say none of these.

screens.why1: Asking how we handled measuring follows from the oversize questions, but it jumps from my last week on the dock to one shipment with no lead-in.
screens.why2: "Your last shipment" and "measuring a sample" don't go together, because one shipment isn't a sample and I run hundreds across a shift, so I can't tell whether you mean that one piece of freight or the whole shift.
screens.why3: I know exactly how we measure on my dock, but only by the shift or the lane, so for a single last shipment I'd be guessing which option fits.
screens.why4: The options describe a shift's worth of freight rather than one shipment and they don't say how it went, though they do cover what we really do, and "Someone else did it" fits since a dimensioner lead or inspector may handle it.
screens.why5: "Measuring a sample" assumes we only sample before I've said so, which puts someone else's framing in my mouth, and it sits oddly beside the option "Only a sample got measured".
screens.why6: It's short and the five options are said as a list, but it's two sentences before the list and "Nothing measured; the paperwork was taken" and "measured only the ones that looked wrong" are a mouthful to hold after one hearing.
screens.instead: On your last shift, how much of the freight got measured? Nearly all of it; most, a few let through; only a sample; only what looked wrong; or none, we went by the paperwork. Or say someone else handled it.
